events.title: Paris–Rouen: reliability before lap times
events.fact: The 1894 Paris–Rouen competition tested practical motor vehicles, not just outright speed.
events.why: Road contests helped demonstrate the new automobile’s capabilities.

events.title: An international organising body
events.fact: The AIACR was founded in Paris by national automobile clubs; it became the FIA in 1946.
events.why: International coordination preceded a single Formula One world championship.

events.title: The ACF Grand Prix in the Sarthe
events.fact: Ferenc Szisz won the 1906 ACF Grand Prix in a Renault.
events.why: Grand Prix organisation developed decades before the world championship.

events.title: Public roads become organised circuits
events.fact: A new Le Mans-area course was designed in 1920, using public roads south of the city.
events.why: Inter-war racing developed venues and organising institutions, well before the F1 world title.

events.title: A European championship before the world title
events.fact: The AIACR’s European Championship preceded the post-war world championship.
events.why: Championship competition did not begin from nothing in 1950.

events.title: War interrupts the European championship
events.fact: The European Championship ended with the outbreak of the Second World War.
events.why: Post-war officials had to rebuild international racing.

events.title: The post-war technical formula
events.fact: After the war, international officials rebuilt Grand Prix rules. Formula One described the leading technical category, distinct from the later championship.
events.why: A formula defines which cars may compete; a championship defines how events award a title.

events.title: A world title is agreed
events.fact: The 1950 drivers’ championship was confirmed in 1949, bringing selected events into a shared title competition.
events.why: Existing Grand Prix racing gained a season-long international championship.

events.title: Silverstone opens the championship
events.fact: Giuseppe Farina won the inaugural championship Grand Prix in an Alfa Romeo. He became the first drivers’ champion later that season.
events.why: This was the championship’s beginning, not the beginning of motor racing or Grand Prix racing.

events.title: Championship races run to Formula Two rules
events.fact: The championship’s principal Grands Prix used Formula Two machinery in 1952 and 1953.
events.why: The world championship and the technical Formula One were not always identical. Indianapolis also had its own rules.

events.title: Mercedes-Benz W196 R
events.fact: The W196 R won on its 1954 French Grand Prix debut. Fangio’s 1954–55 titles established its place in championship history.
events.why: An eight-cylinder powertrain and carefully developed bodywork targeted the performance opportunities of the period’s formula. A museum specification describes one preserved configuration, not every race evolution.

events.title: Constructors gain their own championship
events.fact: A championship for constructors was introduced in 1958, eight years after the drivers’ competition began.
events.why: Teams could now compete for a distinct season title alongside their drivers.

events.title: A rear-engined champion
events.fact: Jack Brabham won the 1959 drivers’ title with Cooper, the first champion in a rear-engined car.
events.why: Moving the engine behind the driver changed packaging, weight distribution and the path toward modern mid-engined layouts.

events.title: Lotus 25: the chassis becomes a shell
events.fact: The Type 25 used a radical semi-monocoque chassis and a 1.5-litre Coventry Climax V8.
events.why: Using the shell to carry loads offered a different route to stiffness and packaging than a frame of tubes.

events.title: Lotus and Clark take the titles
events.fact: The Lotus 25 helped Jim Clark and Team Lotus secure the 1963 drivers’ and constructors’ championships.
events.why: The new chassis architecture had translated into championship success.

events.title: Lotus 49
events.fact: The Type 49 won its first Grand Prix at Zandvoort in 1967 with the new Cosworth DFV.
events.why: Integrating engine and car design reduced compromises between powertrain packaging and the rest of the machine.

events.title: Wings reshape the engineering problem
events.fact: Lotus’s engineering history identifies aerofoil wings on the Type 49 in 1968.
events.why: Aerodynamic load created new demands on structures, suspension and tyre behaviour.

events.title: Renault introduces turbocharging
events.fact: Renault’s RS01 introduced turbocharging to Formula 1 in 1977.
events.why: Exhaust-driven compression offered a route to high output from a smaller engine, with major thermal and reliability challenges.

events.title: Lotus 79
events.fact: The Type 79 developed the ground-effect architecture of the Type 78.
events.why: Longer Venturi tunnels and improved skirts sought stronger underbody performance while reducing drag. Moving fuel into a central cell also changed packaging.

events.title: McLaren MP4/1: carbon composite chassis
events.fact: John Barnard’s MP4/1 brought a carbon-composite chassis into world-championship race use; John Watson won the 1981 British Grand Prix.
events.why: Composite construction allowed a compact structure with high stiffness for its weight.

events.title: Flat-bottom floor rules
events.fact: Flat-bottom rules replaced the previous ground-effect floor approach for 1983.
events.why: Regulators responded to rising cornering speeds; teams had to redesign their cars.

events.title: McLaren MP4/4
events.fact: The MP4/4 won 15 of the 16 championship races in 1988. Senna took the drivers’ title; McLaren the constructors’ championship.
events.why: A turbo engine had to work with tight fuel and boost constraints. Success depended on the complete package, not peak power alone.

events.title: Turbo engines are banned
events.fact: Turbocharged engines were banned for the 1989 season.
events.why: Power, safety and cost concerns had already prompted restrictions; the new formula changed the development priorities.

events.title: Williams FW14B
events.fact: The FW14B won ten races in 1992, nine with Mansell, who secured the drivers’ championship.
events.why: Active suspension helped control the aerodynamic platform while the Renault engine and semi-automatic gearbox contributed to the package.

events.title: Active suspension and electronic aids restricted
events.fact: Active suspension and other electronic driver aids were banned for 1994.
events.why: Rules can remove a successful technology and force teams to solve vehicle-control problems differently.

events.title: Narrower cars and grooved tyres
events.fact: The 1998 rules reduced car width and introduced grooved tyres.
events.why: Regulatory control of tyre and chassis geometry targeted performance rather than a single engine technology.

events.title: Ferrari F2004
events.fact: Schumacher won 13 races in the F2004 on the way to his seventh and final drivers’ title.
events.why: Sustaining dominance required a complete race package: speed, durability and consistent execution rather than a single isolated invention.

events.title: Brawn BGP 001
events.fact: Brawn’s debut Australian Grand Prix produced a one-two finish after Honda’s withdrawal and the team’s rescue.
events.why: The double diffuser exploited an interpretation of the new aerodynamic rules, making regulatory detail part of the engineering opportunity.

events.title: Kinetic energy recovery becomes an option
events.fact: The 2009 changes allowed KERS and brought slick tyres back.
events.why: Braking energy could be recovered and redeployed, adding another energy-management trade-off.

events.title: Mercedes W05 Hybrid
events.fact: The W05 delivered 16 wins, 18 poles and both 2014 world titles.
events.why: A new hybrid formula demanded close integration of combustion, electrical systems, cooling and chassis packaging. The team’s engine programme evolved from an early inline-four concept to a V6.

events.title: Halo cockpit protection arrives
events.fact: The Halo cockpit protection device was introduced in Formula 1 in 2018.
events.why: Head protection became part of the car’s safety architecture, alongside the survival cell and crash structures.

events.title: 2022 ground-effect regulation study
events.fact: The 2022 rules shifted more aerodynamic work toward shaped underfloor tunnels and introduced 18-inch wheel rims.
events.why: The intent was to make the following car less sensitive to the disturbed air behind another car.

events.title: A new active-aerodynamics era
events.fact: The 2026 framework introduces movable front and rear wings and revised power units.
events.why: The December 2025 overview explains the planned high- and low-downforce configurations. It is an overview, not a substitute for the current technical rules.

cars.name: Alfa Romeo 158
cars.drivers: Giuseppe Farina, Luigi Fagioli, Juan Manuel Fangio
cars.story: A pre-war design became the benchmark at the opening championship race. Farina led Alfa Romeo’s Silverstone victory in 1950.
cars.problem: Supercharging increased the mass of air admitted to a small engine. The 158 combined that approach with a front-engine layout and rear-wheel drive.
cars.legacy: Its success connects pre-war Grand Prix machinery with the new drivers’ championship.

cars.problem: An eight-cylinder powertrain and carefully developed bodywork targeted the performance opportunities of the period’s formula. A museum specification describes one preserved configuration, not every race evolution.
cars.legacy: A reminder that circuit needs and engine development create different configurations within one car family.

cars.name: Lotus 25
cars.story: The Type 25 made its breakthrough in 1962; Clark and Lotus took both championships in 1963.
cars.problem: A stressed shell can resist bending and twisting while reducing the volume devoted to a conventional tube frame. That makes chassis architecture an aerodynamic packaging decision too.
cars.legacy: Monocoque construction became a central design approach in Formula 1.

cars.problem: Integrating engine and car design reduced compromises between powertrain packaging and the rest of the machine.
cars.legacy: The DFV became inseparable from the story of the late-1960s and 1970s grid.

cars.problem: Longer Venturi tunnels and improved skirts sought stronger underbody performance while reducing drag. Moving fuel into a central cell also changed packaging.
cars.legacy: Underfloor flow and the quality of the car’s seal to the road became central engineering concerns.

cars.name: McLaren MP4/1
cars.story: Designed by John Barnard, the MP4/1 won the 1981 British Grand Prix with John Watson.
cars.problem: A narrow chassis needed adequate torsional stiffness. Carbon composite offered a new way to achieve that combination.
cars.legacy: Its success and crash survival helped demonstrate the value of composite chassis construction. McLaren’s account also discusses the contemporary Lotus 88; simple “first carbon car” labels need that context.

specs.label: Structure
specs.text: Carbon-composite monocoque; early construction used five major flat-faced components

cars.problem: A turbo engine had to work with tight fuel and boost constraints. Success depended on the complete package, not peak power alone.
cars.legacy: A highly integrated chassis, powertrain and driver pairing defined the last season before the 1989 turbo ban.

cars.name: 2026 regulation study / Mercedes W17 example
cars.drivers: George Russell, Andrea Kimi Antonelli (W17 example)
cars.story: The 2026 formula combines revised hybrid power units with active aerodynamic surfaces. This exhibit uses published W17 specifications as a named example, not a specification for every constructor.
cars.problem: Removing the MGU-H and increasing electrical capability changes energy management. Moving front and rear wings changes the car’s drag/downforce configuration.
cars.legacy: Read each figure in its published context: regulations and in-season implementation can be revised. The creator model is a visual representation, not official engineering CAD.
